## 9. Same-player input ownership and action executor

Implement an explicit input-ownership state machine. Suggested states:

```text
OFF
READY
ACTIVE
PAUSED
MANUAL_OVERRIDE
EMERGENCY_LATCHED
FAULTED
```

### Required key mappings

Register client-side Fabric key mappings:

```text
F8 = toggle AI control
F9 = unconditional local emergency stop
G  = open MinecraftML goal/control screen
```

Make them visible under a MinecraftML controls category and provide translation strings.

### AI off

When the AI is off:

- Never set movement, attack, use, sprint, sneak, jump, or hotbar key states.
- Never rotate the player/camera.
- Never cancel normal user interactions.
- Telemetry may remain connected at a low bounded cadence, but no action may execute.

### AI on

For MVP action execution, support:

- `control`: hold only validated movement states for an exact number of client ticks.
- `look_delta`: apply a bounded camera/player yaw and pitch change on the client thread.
- `sequence`: execute up to three validated `control`/`look_delta`/`noop` primitives under one action ID, with no nesting.
- `stop`: abort and clean up everything the AI owns.
- `noop`: produce a correlated transition without changing controls.

Use the current character’s Minecraft key bindings and player yaw/pitch. Do not send OS-level keystrokes as the normal control mechanism.

### Release-all routine

Create one idempotent `releaseAllAiControls(reason)` routine and call it from every exit path. At minimum it must release:

```text
forward
back
left
right
jump
sneak
sprint
attack
use item
pick block
any AI-selected temporary key state
```

It must also:

- stop sprinting if AI initiated it
- cancel AI-owned block breaking if any started later
- cancel the active executor state machine
- clear queued actions
- mark movement/digging/container activity false
- avoid closing or modifying a user-owned screen unless the AI explicitly opened it
- remain safe when player/world/interaction manager are null

Call it immediately on:

```text
F8 toggle off
F9 emergency stop
manual input override
brain disconnect
deadman timeout
invalid protocol message
stale/conflicting action
world unload or server disconnect
player death/respawn transition
Minecraft focus loss
opening a non-MinecraftML GUI while active
uncaught executor exception
client shutdown
```

### F9 emergency stop

F9 must be entirely local and must work when:

- the Python process is frozen
- the WebSocket is disconnected
- an action future never completes
- protocol parsing is failing

F9 must immediately release controls, cancel the current action, clear queues, and enter a latched emergency state. Reconnection or F8 must not silently clear the latch. Require an explicit `Clear Emergency Stop` action in the G screen before the AI can be re-enabled.

A best-effort emergency/cancel message may be sent to Python afterward, but local safety must not depend on it.

### Brain deadman

While AI control is active, use a conservative deadman timer based on valid heartbeats/messages. If the brain connection is lost or unresponsive beyond the configured threshold, release controls and fault/pause locally. Do not keep walking based on a stale command.

### Manual override

Physical keyboard or mouse input must immediately return control to the user when configured (enabled by default).

Do not detect manual override by reading Minecraft key-binding state after the AI has set it; that cannot distinguish AI state from hardware state. Detect raw hardware input before AI injection using an appropriate client-side input hook or narrowly scoped mixin/callback. Requirements:

- Detect hardware edges for normal movement/action keys.
- Detect meaningful mouse movement/button input.
- Exclude F8, F9, G, and interaction with the MinecraftML screen from accidental override.
- On override: release all AI controls, send best-effort pause/cancel, display the reason, and require F8 or the screen to resume.
- Keep mixins minimal and document why each is needed.

### Threading and queues

- Network thread: parse, size-check, validate, enqueue.
- Client tick: dequeue at most a bounded number of messages, read state, execute actions, collect snapshots.
- Render/HUD: read immutable status snapshots only.
- Use bounded queues and reject/fault on overflow rather than exhausting memory.

Known fake/stubbed runtime behavior

AiControlManager.simulateKeyPress, simulateKeyRelease, applyMouseLookDelta, and resetMouseLook only print messages. They do not control Minecraft.

MinecraftMLMod.showGoalScreen() explicitly says “in a real implementation” and only prints chat/status lines; it is not a GUI.

MouseInputMixin.onCursorPos() always passes (0, 0), so mouse-motion override cannot work.

Brain disconnect/error handling is inconsistent and must always fail closed.

Known action-execution defects

BrainWebSocketClient bypasses the tick-based executeAction path and directly mutates control setters from a background message-processing thread. All Minecraft state and key changes must be marshalled to the client thread.

Timed control actions do not reliably release the key when their duration ends.

Sequence execution changes the state to EXECUTING_CONTROL/EXECUTING_LOOK_DELTA, then checks for EXECUTING_SEQUENCE, making continuation logic invalid.

The action executor reads client.world.getTime() without safely handling menus/world unloads.

There is no complete, correlated action lifecycle result sent back to the Python brain after each action.

There must be one active action at a time, a unique action_id, exactly one terminal result or cancel acknowledgment, and deterministic cleanup.

Known protocol incompatibilities

Java calls its protocol "2.0" and sends a handshake object with version, role, and capabilities.

Python brain/protocol.py currently declares PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1, requires role mineflayer_adapter, and expects a hello message containing client, adapter_version, adapter_id, and session_id.

Java observations use {"type":"observation","tick":...,"data":...} while Python validates request_id, timestamp_ms, and state.

Python sends {"type":"action","action_id":...,"action":{...}}, while Java parses the top-level type as the action type. It would interpret "action" as an unknown action.

Java's control validator expects key and pressed, but BrainWebSocketClient.handleControlAction expects a set of boolean fields such as forward, back, and jump.

FabricProtocolV2 and ProtocolV2 duplicate and contradict each other.

The Java side does not implement the rich result, cancel_ack, and lifecycle data that the Python validator requires.

The protocol must have one canonical schema, shared fixtures, and parity tests on both sides.

3. Implement real same-player input ownership

Replace every logging-only input method with real client-thread behavior.

Use Minecraft's client key bindings and player rotation APIs appropriate for Yarn 1.21.4. The implementation must:

Set and clear the current player's forward, back, left, right, jump, sneak, sprint, attack, and use bindings.

Apply bounded yaw/pitch changes to the same local player/camera.

Track exactly which inputs the AI owns.

F8 off

F9

manual override

brain disconnect/error

protocol error

screen/menu opening where automation is unsafe

world unload/disconnect

player death

mod shutdown

Never call Minecraft player/world/key APIs from the WebSocket listener thread. Decode/validate there, then enqueue immutable commands and consume them on the client tick.

Avoid synthetic OS-level input. Control only the local Minecraft client via supported client APIs.

Never alter another process or send keys outside Minecraft.

Input-control behavior

A timed key action must have deterministic semantics:

accept action
→ capture before_state
→ press requested AI keys on client thread
→ hold for duration_ticks
→ release those keys automatically
→ wait one settling tick when needed
→ capture after_state
→ emit exactly one terminal result

A sequence must preserve parent action_id, execute children in order, respect bounded delays, release inputs between incompatible steps, and produce one terminal result for the parent.

Reject overlapping actions with a clear busy result rather than silently dropping them.

4. Make safety real and local

F8

When OFF and the brain handshake is complete, F8 enters ACTIVE.

When OFF and not connected, F8 may initiate connection but must remain READY/CONNECTING until acknowledgment; it must not falsely display ACTIVE.

When ACTIVE, F8 stops/cancels the current action, releases all inputs locally, informs the brain if possible, and ends in OFF or READY.

F8 must work even if the network thread is stalled.

F9

F9 is an unconditional local emergency stop:

same client tick:
  latch emergency
  cancel local executor
  clear queued actions
  release every key/button
  stop camera changes
  disable AI

It must not wait for or depend on Python, WebSocket acknowledgments, or a database write.

Use explicit latch behavior. A deliberate reset action should return to OFF; it must not accidentally re-enable AI with the same keypress.

Manual override

The first genuine physical input on any currently bound movement/action key, mouse button, or meaningful mouse motion while ACTIVE must:

release all AI inputs
cancel the active action
clear queued actions
enter MANUAL_OVERRIDE or OFF
return control to the user

Requirements:

Honor the user's current rebound key mappings, not getDefaultKey().

React to physical PRESS/REPEAT as appropriate, not RELEASE noise.

Track real cursor deltas; do not pass (0, 0).

Do not interpret the mod's own KeyBinding#setPressed calls as physical user input.

Do not require a double press or two events within 100 ms.

Add tests for rebound keys and first-event takeover.

Deadman

If the brain connection is lost or no valid heartbeat/observation-action traffic is received for a bounded timeout while ACTIVE, stop and release locally. Make the timeout visible in config and HUD.

7. Make exploration learning genuine but deliberately small

This phase is not “general Minecraft AI.” Implement a defensible contextual exploration-bandit loop for a small action library.

Suggested arms:

forward
forward_jump
turn_left_forward
turn_right_forward
turn_slight_left_forward
turn_slight_right_forward
turn_around_forward

Each selected arm must map to a bounded tick-based action or sequence.

Transition boundary

Exactly one learning transition is:

validated observation before
→ choose one arm
→ issue one unique action_id
→ execute in Minecraft
→ receive one terminal result with after_state
→ calculate reward from the measured delta
→ persist one skill_attempt
→ persist one policy_update
→ atomically update one arm

Never update the learner on a timer while the action is still running.

Reward

Base reward only on measurable game changes. Do not use absolute distance from world origin and do not use randomness in reward.

A reasonable initial formula is:

+ horizontal displacement, capped per action
+ new coarse navigation cells/chunks visited
+ small novelty for newly observed block/biome categories
- attempted movement with negligible displacement
- collision/stuck result
- health loss
- dangerous fall/fire/drowning state
- death
- action failure, cancellation, timeout, or unsafe continuation
- excessive action duration

Record the full reward breakdown in SQLite so it is auditable.

Track episode origin and visited coarse cells for this session. Reset episode-local coverage correctly on a new world/session while preserving learned policy values.

Persistence

Use an atomic temporary-file + fsync/replace pattern for policy JSON.

Keep a backup of the last valid policy.

Validate loaded policy schema/version.

Do not use INSERT OR REPLACE to hide duplicates.

Add uniqueness constraints where action IDs must be unique.

Fix ExperienceStore.count() with fetchone()[0].

Use transactions.

Store database and policy under the configured data directory.
